title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Organisms typically rely on surface receptors to perceive and respond to a wide range of environmental signals. While animals primarily use G-protein-coupled receptors, plants predominantly employ receptor-like kinases (RLKs) for signal transduction (Hanlon and Andrew, 2015). RLKs are ubiquitous in plants and regulate essential processes including cell division, development, flowering, and responses to biotic and abiotic stresses (Li and Tax, 2013). The extensive expansion and diversification of RLKs across the plant lineage likely reflect an evolutionary adaptation to a sessile lifestyle, where direct and continuous monitoring of the extracellular environment is essential (Liu et al., 2024a;Tang et al., 2017). Understanding RLK diversity, function, and evolution is therefore central to elucidating plant environmental adaptation. Initial classification of RLKs was established in Arabidopsis thaliana, where the gene family was identified as a plant-specific clade related to animal receptor kinase (Shiu and Bleecker, 2001).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: The significantly larger number of RLKs in plants compared to J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f receptor kinase in animals suggests either plant-specific expansion following the divergence of the two kingdoms or extensive gene loss in animals (Lehti-Shiu and Shiu, 2012;Shiu and Bleecker, 2001). The widely adopted RLK classification system proposed by Shiu has served as a framework for nearly two decades, grouping RLKs into distinct families based on their domains, particularly in model plant species (Shiu and Bleecker, 2001). Building on this framework, recent large-scale analyses incorporated the domain to refine RLK classification. For example, Yin et al. classified 220,038 RLKs from 300 plant species into 18 families using sequence-based methods (Yin et al., 2024). Similarly, we analyzed 311,581 RLKs from over 500 plant genomes, assigning them to 21 known families and annotating 416 domains, resulting in the metaRLK database (Liu et al., 2024b). Despite these advances, 40,357 RLKs (13.0%) remain unclassified and may represent highly divergent members of known families or entirely novel lineages.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: The three-dimensional (3D) structure of a protein is inherently linked with its biological function. Structure-based methods enable precise domain-level analyses of protein structure and function (Holm, 2022;Zhu et al., 2023). However, traditional methods are computationally intensive and unsuitable for large-scale studies (Holm, 2020;Shindyalov and Bourne, 1998;Zhang and Skolnick, 2005). Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have revolutionized structure-based domain parsing and comparison, such as UniDoc and Foldseek (Heinzinger et al., 2024;Van Kempen et al., 2024;Zhu et al., 2023). In parallel, deep learning-based models provide new opportunities for functional inference of uncharacterized proteins (Gane et al., 2022).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Here, we integrated a structure-based strategy encompassing structure-based alignment, structure similarity network analysis and deep learning-based functional clues prediction tools to annotate and classify RLKs in metaRLK database. This approach expanded the diversity of RLK domains and revealed their fold characteristics. We constructed an interactive structure similarity network encompassing over 300,000 RLKs and identified 70 putative new RLK families, 50 of which are associated with plant cell wall-related processes. Our data mining and analysis results are publicly accessible via the metaRLK 2.0 web portal (http://www.metarlk.com).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Result A structure-based alignment for domain annotation in RLKs
text: In metaRLK 2.0, we compiled a comprehensive dataset of 311,581 RLKs from 508 plant species (Table S1). While traditional sequence-based methods classified these RLKs into 21 known families (Liu et al., 2024b), 40,357 RLKs (13.0%) remained unclassified due to a lack of clear family assignments (Table S2). Given the intrinsic relationship between 3D structure and protein function, we implemented a structurebased strategy to enhance domain detection and refine family classification. To achieve this, we applied a structure-guided annotation pipeline: the extracellular part of RLKs with 3D structures (n = 136,766) were segmented into domain units using UniDoc and subsequently annotated by Foldseek, while RLKs lacking 3D structure (n = 174,815) were annotated directly by Foldseek without prior domain units parsing (Fig. 1A). This pipeline identified 677 distinct domains of RLKs, of which 467 were uniquely discovered through the structure-based alignment, representing a 62.7% increase in domain types compared to the sequence-based alignment (Liu et al., 2024b) (Fig. 1B & Table S3). Notably, structural domain annotation enabled the reclassification of 8,998

section: Result A structure-based alignment for domain annotation in RLKs
text: (2.9%) previously unassigned RLKs into existing families, by identifying structurally conserved domains that were undetectable or ambiguous at the sequence level (Table S4). Domain annotation by both sequence-and structure-based alignments were primarily composed of functionally essential and evolutionarily conserved types, including leucine-rich repeat (LRR: PF13855, PF14580, PF08263, PF13306, PF20141, PF12799), malectin (PF11721), legume lectin (L-LEC: PF00139), and cysteine-rich repeat (CRR: PF01657) domain (Fig. 1C; Table S5). These domains are widely distributed across plant lineages and play central roles in immune signaling, cell-surface recognition, and developmental regulation (Shiu and Bleecker, 2001;Zhang et al., 2016).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Result A structure-based alignment for domain annotation in RLKs
text: The structure-based method uniquely identified 467 novel domains, revealing a significant, underappreciated layer of RLK diversity. Remarkably, eight of these structurally-defined domains were highly abundant, each comprising over 1,000 members despite being entirely absent from traditional sequence-based alignment (Fig. 1D). Interestingly, four of these domains belonged to the β-propeller domains (Pfam J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f clan: CL0186) which have high-symmetry architectures (Fig. 1D). The β-propeller domains are structurally stable but display substantial sequence variability (Bonnardel et al., 2019). As a result, they can be reliably detected by structure-based alignment but often evade sequence-based identification (average sequence identity = 0.11). This property likely explains why RLKs annotated as the representative β-propeller domain regulator of chromosome condensation 1 (RCC1: PF00415, PF13540) by sequencebased alignments are further resolved into more than 10 distinct β-propeller domain types in structure-based alignment.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: To adapt to the diverse and complex extracellular environment, plant RLKs often incorporate multi-domains (≥ 2, e.g. S-domain) which enhances or diversifies their functional capabilities (Dievart et al., 2020). Before domain annotation, we employed a structure-based domain segmentation method, guided by the principle of structural biology, to precisely delineate multi-domain RLKs into their individual domain units (Fig. 1A). This facilitates accurate domain-based structural and functional studies.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: We annotated a total of 66,632 multi-domain across 136,766 RLKs with 3D structures. Across these multidomain RLKs, architectures composed of two domain units were the most prevalent (Fig. S1). To assess how structure-based domain segmentation improves structural resolution and functional interpretability, we compared these annotations with those derived from sequence-based method (Liu et al., 2024b). Overall, 54,200 J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f RLKs (81.3%) showed consistent family assignments between the two methods, including 39,583 classified as LRR-RLKs. While these RLKs were annotated as singledomain by sequence analysis, structure-based segmentation revealed that they contain multiple tandem, independently folded LRR units (Fig. S1C-I). Importantly, structurebased segmentation uncovered additional domains in 1,897 RLKs (2.9%) that were missed by sequence-based annotation. For example, 63 RLKs previously classified as LRR-type were found to harbor an additional pkinase domain (Fig. S1C-II). Moreover, 528 RLKs that lacked any domain annotation by sequence-based methods were resolved as LRR-RLKs through structural analysis (Fig. S1C-IV).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Therefore, the refined domain segmentation does not alter RLK family classification but substantially enhances domain resolution and functional interpretability.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Interestingly, structure-based analysis also revealed rare configurations involving Glyco_hydro_16 (PF00722) and WAK domains (Table S6). The former forms a repetitive α/β-fold architecture, while the latter adopts a rigid β-fold. This pairing reflects a fold-level contrast and suggests potential functional interplay between flexible enzymatic modules and rigid recognition scaffolds.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: The RLK domains act as modular building blocks that mediate extracellular signal perception. The internal fold architecture of domain defines its structural configuration, which in turn determines its stability, flexibility, and potential binding specificity. To investigate how folds are distributed across RLK domains, we performed domain-level fold classification using the CATH hierarchy (Lau et al., 2024;Sillitoe et al., 2021) (Table S7). We identified 31 folds in total, with β-folds being the most numerous, comprising 16 types, including multiple β-hairpins or β-propellers, as well as the more rigid β-barrels (Fig. 2A&B). Additionally, eight α/β folds (e.g., α/β horseshoe and α/β barrel) and four α folds were detected, the latter being largely confined to extracellular protein kinases (PF00069, PF07714) (Table S8).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: Among the most prevalent domains-LRR, typically adopting an α/β fold that forms a horseshoe-like structure involved in ligand recognition (Kobe and Deisenhofer, 1996;Liu et al., 2008) (Fig. 2A). The LRR-RLKs such as BRI1 (Locus ID: At4g39400), parallel β-sheets form a stable scaffold, while α-helices confer flexibility, together J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f creating a concave binding surface optimized for ligand interaction (Hothorn et al., 2011;She et al., 2011). Another representative α/β fold is the α/β barrel, such as Glyco_hydro_18 (PF00704) domain in glycoside hydrolases. These enzymes regulate cell wall remodeling by catalyzing polysaccharide metabolism (Hurtado-Guerrero et al., 2009;Rai et al., 2016). The α/β barrel fold consists of a central β-barrel forming an enclosed barrel, which is surrounded by eight α-helices on the outside. This highly symmetrical structure provides both rigidity and enzymatic precision, with a central catalytic pocket that remains stable even in the complex extracellular environments (Fig. 2C).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: Notably, our structure-based analysis uncovered a much broader diversity of β-folds than previously recognized. Previously, β-folds in RLKs were predominantly represented by the β-hairpins arrangements found in WAK domains (Zhang et al., 2005).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: Notably, we found that some pore-forming architectures within the domain adopt βbarrel structures, a feature commonly associated with proteins in animals and microorganisms (Zhang and Han, 2016). These include domains such as Porin_3 (PF01459), OmpA_membrane (PF01389), and Omp85 (PF01103) (Fig. 2D). The Porin_3 domain is typically found in the mitochondrial outer membrane of eukaryotes and facilitates passive diffusion of small hydrophilic molecules such as ATP, ADP, and phosphate (Shoshan- Barmatz and Ben-Hail, 2012). OmpA_membrane and Omp85 domains are best known from bacterial outer membranes. OmpA interacts with the peptidoglycan layer to provide mechanical strength (Reusch, 2012), while Omp85 facilitates β-barrel insertion and protein translocation (Doyle and Bernstein, 2022). These β-barrel domains in plant RLKs may contribute to extracellular structural support or facilitate protein localization at the cell surface.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: Many β-fold domains, such as L-LEC and Peptidase_S9_N, are composed of multiple β-hairpins or β-propeller architectures. These domains are known to mediate interactions with complex extracellular macromolecules: L-LEC domains act as carbohydrate-binding modules that recognize glycoproteins or polysaccharides, such as pectin or xyloglucans (Damme et al., 1998); and Peptidase_S9_N domains, as seen in animal DPPIV enzymes, engage in protein-protein or protein-peptide interactions through their β-propeller substructures (Aertgeerts et al., 2005). Notably, β-propeller domains were substantially expanded by structural-based method. These domains J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f exhibited diverse symmetry patterns-including 3-, 5-, and 7-bladed configurationsrather than strictly canonical forms (Fig. 2E & Fig. S2), suggesting functional specialization or modular diversification among RLK subtypes. Strikingly, we identified a previously unreported architecture: a mirrored dual 3-fold β-propeller composed of two tandem, symmetric three-bladed units (Fig. 2E).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: This fold likely arose through duplication and fusion events, conferring enhanced structural stability and an enlarged interface for multivalent ligand recognition. Collectively, these observations support the notion that β-fold-rich domains are particularly well suited for stable, multivalent recognition of large and heterogeneous ligands in extracellular environments. Their rigid architectures reduce conformational entropy loss upon binding, potentially enhancing both affinity and specificity.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Enrichment of rigid β-Fold architectures in RLK domains
text: Taken together, these results reveal a surprising dominance of structurally rigid β-fold architectures in RLKs, challenging traditional assumptions of α/β fold prevalence and underscoring the structural and functional diversity encoded within plant receptor systems (Lehti-Shiu et al., 2009).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: The uncharacterized RLKs remain resistant to classification due to limited homology 3D templates-hereafter referred to as "dark RLKs". To overcome this limitation, we constructed the first large-scale structural similarity network of RLKs, allowing us to explore potential family relationships and functional clustering beyond conventional annotation pipelines.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: We first performed structure-based clustering of all RLKs and retained 6,753 clusters (encompassing 98.8% of all RLKs) that contained at least two RLKs. Based on the structural similarity between the representative of clusters (Durairaj et al., 2023), we constructed a structural similarity network comprising 6,179 connected nodes and approximately 1.05 million edges (Fig. 3A), which successfully incorporated 34,227 dark RLKs (94.5%).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: The network contained 124 components with at least two nodes, with the largest (component 1) encompassing about 92.2% of all nodes (Fig. 3A; Table S9). Further modular analysis of component 1 revealed distinct 12 communities, in which 19 known J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f RLK families were tightly clustered. Many communities were highly enriched for a single family: community 6 was dominated by LRR family (98.8%), community 7 by L-LEC family (97.8%), and community 8 by Xiao family (93.0%) (Table S9). In particular, component 2 formed a well-separated subnetwork composed predominantly of the Xiang family (93.3%) (Fig. 3A). These results corroborate the previously reported sequence-based classification by Liu et al. and provide independent structural evidence that Xiao and Xiang constitute evolutionarily distinct and well-defined RLK families (Liu et al., 2024b).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Although not all subnetworks were dominated by a single family (Table S9), family members tended to form compact and minimally overlapping clusters, reflecting strong intra-family structural conservation and the robustness of the network (Fig. 3A). These characteristics provided a solid framework for the discovery of novel RLK families and for reclassifying previously unannotated dark RLKs within an evolutionary context.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Reassignment of dark RLKs through network-based prediction
text: Within the structural similarity network, 25,933 dark RLKs clustered in component 1 and 2, yet could not be reliably annotated using structure-based alignment alone (Fig. S3). To overcome this, we applied ProtNLM-based functional clue prediction and compared the inferred functional profiles of dark RLKs with those of known families within the same network communities. When functional predictions were consistent, dark RLKs were reassigned accordingly. Using this integrative strategy, 18,571 dark RLKs in community 3 were reassigned to the WAK family, 1,306 in community 10 to the Lysin-Motif (LysM) family, and 3,225 in communities 5, 6, and 11 to the LRR family (Fig. 3B & Table S10). Applying the same method to components 2 further reassigned 301 dark RLKs to the Xiang family. In total, 23,403 dark RLKs (90.2%) were successfully reclassified.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Reassignment of dark RLKs through network-based prediction
text: Overall, this network-guided integration of structural clustering and functional inference provides a scalable framework for resolving the biological identity of dark RLKs beyond the limits of sequence-or structure-only methods.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Unclassifiable RLKs: The remaining dark space
text: Despite integrating structural annotation, clustering-based network, and large language J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f model-based functional clues prediction, 6,792 dark RLKs remained unclassified, lacking confident family assignments or predictive functional clues (Table S11). These dark RLKs represent a substantial unresolved region of the RLK landscape.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Unclassifiable RLKs: The remaining dark space
text: Among them, 1,963 dark RLKs formed singleton clusters and were excluded from the network. The remaining 4,829 dark RLKs within the structural similarity network were grouped into three categories: first, 2,031 RLKs appeared as isolated nodes in network; second, 248 RLKs which from different components, lacking links to known RLK families and showing inconsistent functional predictions (Table S11); third, 2,550 RLKs were connected to multiple known RLK families but lacked consistent functional signatures. Among the 752 of these RLKs with available structures, UniDoc segmentation revealed that 578 could be partitioned into multiple domain units, potentially explaining their broad structural similarity across different families. To enhance classification accuracy, we integrated findings from Liu et al. study (Liu et al., 2024b), reclassified 1,885 dark RLKs (Table S11).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Based on the structural similarity network, we observed that many RLK families formed distinct and well-separated subnetworks (Fig. 3A). We defined a novel RLK family when a subnetwork (each with ≥ 2 nodes and ≥ 10 RLKs) contained more than 80% of similar domains or dark RLKs. For example, community 9-comprising 83.2% β-propeller domains (Pfam clan: CL0186)-was designated as a new β-propeller RLK family, incorporating 34 structurally distinct β-propeller domains (Table S2). Using the same criteria, 2,565 dark RLKs were grouped into 68 small, disconnected components that showed no detectable similarity to known RLK families (Fig. 3C & Table S9).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Unlike these independently clustered families, pkinase domains (highlighted in red in Fig. 3A) are widely distributed across multiple subnetworks but predominantly converge at the center of the network. These "pkinase" nodes exhibit the highest average betweenness centrality among all RLK families, suggesting that they serve as key structural bridges connecting distinct RLK families (Fig. 3A; Table S12). Although they do not form an isolated subnetwork or represent a dominant family, their cohesive distribution pattern and central location indicate shared structural features and potential functional significance. Based on their network topological characteristics, we J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f therefore classify them as a novel RLK family-the Pkinase family (Table S2).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Taken together, the 68 isolated subnetworks, along with the β-propeller and Pkinase families, led to the definition of 70 novel RLK families. This represents a 333.3% increase in RLK family diversity compared to previous classifications (Fig. 3D), substantially expanding our understanding of RLK structural and evolutionary complexity.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Distribution and evolutionary patterns of RLK families
text: Among the 91 identified RLK families-comprising 21 known and 70 newly defined families-we found that 15 were broadly distributed across more than 400 plant species.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Distribution and evolutionary patterns of RLK families
text: These include well-established groups such as LRR, WAK, Malectin-like, L-LEC, Xiao, and Xiang families (Fig. 4A& Fig. S4).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Distribution and evolutionary patterns of RLK families
text: The LRR family emerged as the most abundant and widespread, present in an average of 507 species. Interestingly, the only exception was Caulerpa lentillifera, which lacked LRR domains entirely; this species contained only a single RLK, whose domain annotated as IL6Ra-bind (PF09240). Other families showing wide distribution include PAN (371 species), Malectin (287 species), Thaumatin (163 species), component 3 (160 species), and component 4 (134 species), underscoring their broad evolutionary presence across the plant kingdom (Fig. S4 & Table S2).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Distribution and evolutionary patterns of RLK families
text: In contrast, the 70 newly identified RLK families exhibit clear lineage specificityexcept for Pkinase and β-propeller, which are broadly distributed, most of the others are enriched in either eudicots or monocots (Fig. S4 & Table S2). Notably, the component 31 and von willebrand factor type A (VWA) families were exclusively found in bryophytes, primarily in Physcomitrella patens. Similarly, the component 72 family, identified in five species, consists exclusively of plants from the Fabaceae family, with four of these species belonging to the Arachis genus (Fig. 4B; Table S2).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Distribution and evolutionary patterns of RLK families
text: These findings suggest that while a core set of RLK families is conserved across land plants, many newly discovered families exhibit clade-specific expansions, likely reflecting lineage-dependent functional diversification.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f
text: To infer the potential functions of newly identified RLK families, including 68 novel families composed of 2,565 dark RLKs and the previously defined Xiao and Xiang families (Liu et al., 2024b), we utilized ProtNLM, which can predict and classify functional clues for dark RLKs with high confidence in a structure similarity network (Fig. 3B).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f
text: Remarkably, ProtNLM predicted that 49 out of the 68 novel families exhibited functional clues associated with vegetative cell wall protein gp1-like (Table S13), which binding oligogalacturonides-degradation products of pectin-thereby participating in cell wall integrity sensing and potentially contributing to salt-alkali stress adaptation in Oryza sativa (Locus ID: Os03g0852400) (Zhu et al., 2024).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f
text: Additionally, functional clues for component 38 were assigned as proline-rich protein HaeIII subfamily 1-like (Boron et al., 2014), further supporting their clues in plant cell wall biology. For four families (component 10, 11, 34, and 119), ProtNLM returned low-confidence outputs, preventing functional assignment (Fig. 5A).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f
text: We also annotated the plant-specific Xiao and Xiang families, originally defined by Liu et al. ProtNLM predicted that Xiao is homologous to ALE2, a protein kinase in Arabidopsis that contains the ALE2-N domain-a structure similar to Xiao despite limited sequence conservation (Fig. 5B&C; Table S13). ALE2 is involved in epidermal differentiation and cuticle formation (Tanaka et al., 2007). Similarly, Xiang was predicted to resemble the SPARK domain (PF19160), which plays a role in plant-fungal symbiosis (Montero et al., 2021) (Fig. 5B&D; Table S13).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: To achieve a more accurate and in-depth understanding of RLKs, we comprehensively upgraded the metaRLK database using structure-based strategy. The updated version, metaRLK 2.0, integrates domain-level structure comparison, fold classification, structural clustering, family grouping, and function prediction. By constructing a structure similarity network and leveraging large language models, we conducted a systematic analysis of RLK families. The database also provides two search tools-Diamond (based on sequence similarity) and Foldseek (based on structural similarity)-to enable flexible and efficient exploration of RLKs. Currently, metaRLK 2.0 includes 883 domains (the combined set derived from both sequence-and structure-J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f based annotation strategies) from 508 plant species, classified into 31 distinct folds and 91 RLK families (including 70 novel identified families) (Fig. 6). The database is freely accessible at www.metaRLK.com. In future updates, we plan to incorporate RLK variant sites, predict potential ligands, and further investigate their biological clues in plants.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: In this study, we comprehensively re-annotated plant RLKs through structure-based analysis, uncovering previously unrecognized layers of domain and family diversity that extend beyond the limits of traditional sequence-based classification (Liu et al., 2024b;Yin et al., 2024). Because protein structures are generally more conserved than sequences, structure-based analysis enables more sensitive detection of domainsparticularly those with divergent sequences or repetitive structural features (Lau et al., 2023). Using this method, we identified 677 distinct domains in RLKs, representing a 62.7% increase over sequence-based method (Liu et al., 2024b). Many of these newly identified domains display repetitive structural motifs, such as β-propeller domains, which were not detected by sequence-based methods. Furthermore, we identified numerous extracellular protein kinase domains; through motif detection (GxGxxG, HRD and DFG motifs), 38.1% of protein kinase domains were marked as pseudokinase.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Interestingly, our findings suggest that some RLK families-particularly those newly identified in this study-may represent lineage-specific or even species-specific innovations. These families often display unique structural characteristics (e.g., isolated subnetworks) and are restricted to specific plant lineages. For example, the VWA family was found here to be present in eight bryophyte species across a dataset of 508 plant species (Fig. 4B & Table S2), reinforcing its bryophyte-specific distribution (Lehti-Shiu and Shiu, 2012). Notably, while the VWA domain has also been detected in higher plants (e.g., Oryza sativa), where its expression is associated with responses to various biotic and abiotic stresses (e.g., pathogens, drought, and salinity) (Karkute et al., 2022).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Additionally, we identified component 31 as another bryophyte-specific RLK family, the functional clues associated with AAI domain-containing proteins, and detected exclusively in six bryophyte species (Fig. 4B & Table S2). Strikingly, ProtNLM predicted that 49 new RLK families were gp1-like, with 41 showing strong lineage J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f specificity (over 90%)-most notably in Brassicaceae (9 families), Poaceae (8 families), Rosaceae (5 families), Fabaceae (5 families), and Malvaceae (5 families) (Table S2). This taxonomically narrow distribution underscores the lineage-specific evolution and possible adaptive specialization of newly defined RLK families.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: However, due to limited sampling and current computational constraints, their fold types and 3D structures remain largely uncharacterized.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: A major and unexpected finding was the enrichment of rigid β-fold architectures, such as β-hairpin, β-propeller and β-barrel structures in RLKs. These structures are potentially involved in interactions with complex extracellular polysaccharides or structural components of the cell wall (Kohorn and Kohorn, 2012;Solan et al., 2021). This is highly consistent with the unique constraints of plant cell biology, in which a rigid extracellular matrix imposes functional demands not present in animal systems.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Unlike animals that predominantly use GPCRs embedded in flexible plasma membranes, plants have evolved RLKs with rigid, repetitive extracellular structures to mediate signal transduction through the cell wall. The functional implications of this adaptation are profound and suggest that RLKs are structurally tailored for robust ligand recognition and mechanical stability in a cell wall-dominated environment.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: While recent advances in large language models offer promising insights into protein functional prediction, these predictions remain preliminary. To enhance their reliability, we integrated them with structural similarity networks and used shared functional patterns within subnetworks to reclassify dark RLKs and infer potential functions for novel families. As research progresses, the functions of these novel families will be better understood, allowing for their renaming. In future work, we plan to validate these functional predictions through experimental methods, such as ligand-binding assays and substrate identification, to clarify the upstream and downstream roles of RLKs.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: In conclusion, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating structure-based alignment, structure similarity networks, and large language model-based functional inference in identifying novel RLK families and domain architectures. Using this expanded framework, we successfully reclassified 25,044 out of the 40,357 RLKs that were previously unannotated by sequence-based methods and defined 70 novel RLK families. These findings not only improve the classification of RLKs but also uncover deep, previously unrecognized evolutionary innovations-particularly among lineage-J o u r n a l P r e -p r o o f specific and structurally atypical receptors. The continued integration of computational predictions with experimental validation will be essential to fully elucidate the biological and evolutionary clues of this highly diverse RLK superfamily.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Sources of RLK data from metaRLK
text: We obtained RLK data for 508 plant species from metaRLK in June 2024 (Liu et al., 2024b). This study focused only on canonical RLKs; therefore, we only selected members from metaRLK if they met the criteria of having an extracellular domain, one transmembrane domain, and one intracellular kinase domain. To ensure data accuracy, we re-employed TMbed (v1.0.0) (python -m tmbed predict -f ./input -p ./result.pred -format 4) to predict the transmembrane topology for RLK members from the metaRLK database, ensuring all members met the requirements (Bernhofer and Rost, 2022).

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
section: Annotation of the RLK domains using Foldseek
text: We applied a structure-guided annotation pipeline: the extracellular part of RLKs with 3D structures (n = 136,766) were segmented into domain units using UniDoc (version 20251022) (Zhu et al., 2023) and subsequently annotated by Foldseek, while RLKs lacking 3D structure (n = 174,815) were annotated directly by Foldseek without prior domain units parsing. The domain parsing command line: python Run_UniDoc_from_scratch_structure.py -i ./input_pdb -c A -o ./result Foldseek (v9.427df8a) was used to align each extracellular part of RLK against the 3D domain dataset (Heinzinger et al., 2024;Van Kempen et al., 2024). We created this dataset of 889,291 3D structure of domains, consisting of PDB and mmCIF files obtained from the PDB database. The mapping data between domain and PDB entries was derived from the SIFTS database in September 2024. We performed a highcoverage, high-sensitivity 3Di/AA-based Foldseek search on the 311,581 RLKs. title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: Step1 (data preparation): foldseek createdb ./clusters ./clusters_db Step2 (alignment): foldseek search ./clusters_db ./domain_db ./result tmp -s 9.5 -c 0.5 -e 0.0001 Step3 (display result): foldseek convertalis ./clusters_db ./domain_db ./result result.m8 We focused particularly on the largest connected component, component 1, which encapsulates the majority of RLK structural diversity. To investigate community structure within this largest component, we performed modularity-based analysis using the louvain R package (v1.4.2). To evaluate the importance of each RLK family within component 1, we calculated the betweenness centrality of each node using the igraph R package (v2.1.4) and computed the average betweenness centrality for each RLK family based on its members.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: For dark RLKs located within subnetworks (components or communities) that contain known RLK families in the structural similarity network, we used ProtNLM web server (https://neurosnap.ai/service/ProtNLM) to predict their functions (Gane et al., 2022). If any of the top5 predicted functional clues matched the known RLK family, the corresponding dark RLK was reassigned to that family.

title: metaRLK 2.0: an updated database of plant receptor-like kinases developed with structure-and deep learning-based functional annotation and classification
text: For the 68 novel RLK families, we excluded uninformative predictions such as "hypothetical protein" or "secreted protein," and selected the top-ranked predicted functional clue-based on both frequency and confidence score-as the representative functional annotation. The same approach was applied to the previously uncharacterized LRR, WAK, LysM, Xiao and Xiang families.
